In standard mathematics, the Category of matrices Mat is the category where the objects are natural numbers and the morphisms are matrices. The idea is that in the same way that the concept of a group can be generalized to a groupoid (which is like a group where the multiplication is a partial function), a monoid can be generalized to a category (which is like a monoid but multiplication is a partial function).

In Lean, we can form matrices with arbitrary finite index types, so our category docs#CategoryTheory.Mat has the type of finite types as objects. This makes it more compatible with Matrix. But I'm not sure this is the best decision. To me, it seems that

  1. It makes the category noncomputable, because the identity morphism is the identity matrix if i = j then 1 else 0 and we can't get a DecidableEq instance from a Fintype instance. A similar situation applies to Mat_, which I need to be computable for a project.
  2. We are tracking an extra universe parameter which doesn't actually do anything. Right now this issue is bypassed by requiring the ring R to live in the same universe as the types.
  3. This could lead to potential equality of types issues down the line. If I remember correctly, Mat_ already uses things like docs#CategoryTheory.eqToHom.

Would it be a good idea to have CategoryTheory.Mat have as objects natural numbers, but then design the API in such a way that pretends that the objects are really finite types? I think this would lead to an equivalent category which is more computable. I am currently writing a computable version of Mat_ called CMat_ for use in a group project, and I don't think this requires changing the API very much.

Of course, if you take this argument to its extreme, this would lead to replacing docs#FintypeCat with the set of natural numbers as well, and this sounds like a disruptive change even if the API remains similar.

@Niels Voss Good question. The proof of the pudding is in the eating...

But let me see if I understand: do you need the entire category to be computable? Or is it enough if you get decidable equality for certain morphisms / vectors / etc...

Because if i = j then 1 else 0 is not a problem if the object you plug in is Fin n.
Using general finite/fintype index types is quite convenient when using block matrices, and it is also more practical when constructing certain structures on Mat_, like (bi)products.

We are working on an algorithm that computes on bounded cochain complexes, so I would need isomorphism of objects to be decidable if the original category has decidable equality of objects. I also need coproducts and composition of morphisms to be computable. But what's best for me might not be best for mathlib.

Using general finite/fintype index types is quite convenient when using block matrices, and it is also more practical when constructing certain structures on Mat_, like (bi)products.

You could design the API in such a way to hide the fact that Mat_ uses Fin or Lists rather than arbitrary Fintypes. This would mean redefining Mat_.ι instead of having it be in the constructor, but still using Mat_.ι in all of the API. The main disadvantage is that you would have to sacrifice the definitional equality Mat_.ι (Mat_.mk T _ f) = T, which would then become a bijection instead.

I don't think the biproducts construction is that big of a deal; in fact, I think defining Mat_ T as a wrapper around List T actually makes coproducts easier to construct and it makes them computable.
Would changing FintypeCat to also bundle DecidableEq make things computable in the way you want? Nevermind, I see that after #36498 FintypeCat only bundles Finite not Fintype
